title: Containers Explained for Teams Shipping Their First Service
content:
Your first service works on one developer's laptop but fails on the deployment host because the runtime and installed libraries differ. A container image can package the service's runtime environment into a repeatable artifact. It does not package away networking, persistent data, secrets, or the responsibility to operate the process.

Distinguish image, container, and host

An image is the packaged filesystem and metadata used to start a container. A container is a running instance with a process, runtime settings, and a writable layer. The host supplies the underlying execution environment. Rebuilding an image and restarting a container are different operations, so record which artifact actually reached production.

Docker introduces containers as isolated processes in its container explanation. They are not simply miniature virtual machines with an independently managed operating-system kernel. Isolation is useful, but running untrusted software with excessive host access still carries risk. Do not treat the word container as a complete security assessment.

Choose one main service responsibility for the first image. Keep the web application separate from an unrelated database or scheduler unless there is a concrete operational reason to combine them. A process that exits should have an observable exit status and a clear restart policy rather than a hidden shell loop that conceals failure.

Build an artifact you can identify

Put the build recipe in version control with the application. Install declared dependencies, copy only the necessary source, and define the startup command explicitly. Exclude local credentials, development exports, caches, and unrelated files from the build context. An ignored application file and an excluded build-context file are separate concerns.

Docker's build guidance covers small trusted base images, multi-stage builds, limited packages, and version pinning. A multi-stage build can keep compilers and other build-only tools out of the final runtime image. That can simplify the artifact without proving the remaining packages are vulnerability-free.

Use a release identifier and preserve the resulting digest. A tag is a name that may later point to different content; a digest identifies specific content. Pinning improves repeatability, but it also means you must deliberately rebuild and adopt updates. Reproducibility is not an excuse to freeze vulnerable dependencies forever.

Supply configuration and secrets at runtime

Build one application artifact and supply environment-specific configuration through the deployment platform's supported mechanism. Keep secrets outside the image and repository. Removing a secret in a later image layer does not make placing it in an earlier layer a safe practice.

Write down required settings, safe defaults, and which missing values should prevent startup. Validate them before accepting traffic. Avoid printing full connection strings or tokens during startup diagnostics. An operator should be able to identify a missing database setting without seeing the password.

Run with the least privileges the service needs. Avoid privileged mode and host-wide mounts for routine application operation. File permissions must match the runtime user, particularly for mounted storage. A service that runs as a non-root user but can access an unnecessary host socket may still have excessive authority.

Decide what survives replacement

Containers are replaceable; customer records are not. Docker's persistence guide explains that changes in a container's writable filesystem disappear when that container is deleted, while volumes have a separate lifecycle. A restart of the same container and deletion followed by replacement are therefore different persistence checks.

Map every write: uploads, database files, generated reports, temporary scratch data, and logs. Put authoritative data in an appropriate managed store or explicitly managed volume. Do not assume a volume is backed up because it survives container replacement. Persistence, replication, and recoverability are separate properties.

Check storage paths against the exact application and database image version. A generic example's mount point may not match your chosen version. Practice replacement with synthetic data before production and confirm that data returns from the intended store rather than from a forgotten container layer.

Hypothetical example: a small image-resizing API

Consider a hypothetical team shipping an API that resizes uploaded photos. Its image contains the runtime, image library, and application code. The deployment supplies the storage destination and limited service credentials. Temporary resizing files use disposable space; original uploads belong in durable storage.

The application listens on the configured interface inside the container. The team separately configures the host or platform's published route and TLS termination. Declaring a port in image metadata alone is not a complete public networking setup. It checks both an internal request and the actual user-facing route.

Before release, the team plans a replacement check: upload a synthetic image, replace the container using the same release configuration, and retrieve the expected output. That would test one persistence path, not establish resilience to all host failures. Recovery of durable storage needs its own procedure.

First container checklist

  • Can the team identify the exact image deployed?
  • Are build-only tools and private local files excluded?
  • Are secrets supplied outside the artifact?
  • Does the runtime user have only necessary privileges?
  • Are durable writes mapped and independently recoverable?
  • Can the process shut down cleanly when asked?
  • Are logs, startup errors, and the real public route observable?

Keep the first deployment understandable. A small service with a documented image, configuration contract, storage map, and replacement procedure is a stronger foundation than an elaborate orchestration stack whose failure behavior nobody can explain.
excerpt: Understand images, runtime configuration, persistent data, networking, and replacement before shipping your first containerized service.
